title: Watched Poor Things yesterday and thought it’s too cynical to my taste…

commenti.body: [removed]

I mean personally I read the film as a socialist work first and foremost. Throughout the work there is a fixation on progress and development and growth first individually and then consequently socially. The world can be improved and Bella’s journey ultimately is about her development as a person which gives her the tools to improve the world later on.

I really like Yorgos' movies, and I saw The Lobster in the theater on a whim and I loved it, but his movies are very different, and are not conventional by any means.  The Favourite might be one you would enjoy more, but I wouldnt recommend The Lobster or Killing of the Sacred Deer to you probably.  I havent seen his Greek movies yet. I would say this is his least bleak movie that I have seen. 

I definitely feel like his movies arent supposed to be scrutinized at a surface level.  Poor things is very fantastical.  It has bits of Frankenstein and Pinocchio, but also a very early 1900's take on futurism, and dreamlike at times.  IDK how to articulate it well, but I thoroughly enjoyed it and it was maybe my favorite of 2023.

Well, what the director tells you and what you get from the movie can obviously differ.

While what you point out is a valid dissonance of sorts, I think the movie wasn't concerned much about that.

Poor Things, is, first and foremost, a study of life. All of its aspects - fear, disappointment, shock, despair, rage, delight, uncertainty, boredom. By observing and experiencing life from various angles, Bella became a human being in her own right and in turn, as Madame Swiney put it, the world became hers.

Moral judgements aside, this movie was about Bella choosing her own place in the world, and she chose what was known to her the most: Godwin's profession and all things related to it. This also introduces the themes of legacy and succession.

There is also the theme of rebirth - Victoria's child living her life as Bella, giving her mother a second existence of sorts.

I totally agree with what you said about "plot armor" protecting Bella from any real consequences/stakes! It not only made the story less compelling, it made the script's would-be feminist moments ring totally hollow because, as you said, this naive young woman goes around putting herself in situations that are extremely dangerous for women, yet she just bops along unscathed, never getting abused (or pregnant) and never having to struggle to accomplish a goal. I *love* "The Favourite" and "Dogtooth" so I was prepared to love this too, but it didn't have a fraction of the emotional heft those movies have for me.

>and now I feel weirder knowing that the director describes this piece of work as positive and hopeful. How on earth could it be hopeful?

To be fair, he said it's *his* most positive and hopeful work. Which I completely agree with, there's an optimism there that isn't really present in much else he's done. Watch Dogtooth or The Killing Of A Sacred Deer and I think you'll understand exactly what he means
[removed]
Dogtooth is an amazing movie that made me feel so uncomfortable and horrified the entire movie. Alps is heartbreaking and beautiful.
Dogtooth is his best work. You need to watch ASAP

The one thing that I don’t understand is why they chose to give the asshole ex husband the goats body instead of giving it to HER FATHER- who she loved- who died exactly the same time so that he could keep living????
I recently watched Dogtooth for the first time, since everyone is recommending it as his best work, but it was my least favourite by far. Not sure if that says more about me or about the film.

If you want to understand how it's his most positive film, watch the others. Simple as that. They are bleak, twisted affairs. ("The Favourite" is still his most palatable imo).

As for how it could be empowering to women: it's certainly a sex-positive, slut-positive movie for one thing. Some folks are behind the ball on this, but treating sex work as work is feminist. The film is also unfailingly scathing toward men as a whole, and I actually think that's who the the title may refer to. By the end, Bella is simply so above it all, weary of and amused by the cluelessness of the men in her life.

I felt it enhanced the fairy-tale feeling of the movie that she *didn't* suffer any lasting negative consequences. There are so many movies and stories already out there that punish women for being promiscuous, so I'm kind of glad they didn't go that route. I don't think we were supposed to take the movie completely seriously either, as if these things are actually happening. The entire movie is larger than live, so I don't think a lack of realism is making the movie worse.

My interpretation is that they let Godwin die as a way to finally give him some relief. Throughout the whole movie, we hear about the guy had been butchered his whole childhood and it left him in a broken state. I imagine the last thing they’d want to do, unless he specifically requested it, is further his trauma from being a walking experiment.
[removed]
Because that's what you *expected.* You were purposefully misled to believe that would happen.

I think The Favourite was much better than Poor Things. I also thought The Favourite suffered from some “here’s a weird thing” moments that felt motivated by the director doing it because he could and not because it aided the story/film in a meaningful way.

I feel like Poor Things was basically nothing but those moments for 2 hours plus 30 minutes of captivating cinema. (Probably the opposite actually but that’s what it felt like).

Good point. I feel like some dialogue from Godwin talking about the finality of death or something was missing to make this make sense. Some sort of “I strove for immortality through my work, but I’m at peace with my own end.” sort of thing.

I can see that, and I'm definitely not lobbying for all female-centric movies to be trauma porn. My quibble is more that the movie *purports* to show Bella making her own way through a dangerous world but the few times she is in danger, luck (or a man) does most of the work for her

The film makes it very clear (at least to me) that Bella is all about autonomy. She’s grateful to be alive, but she’s upset that she didn’t have any say in what Godwin did to bring her to the world. And yes, she has forgiven him, but she doesn’t want to be a part of the problem by giving him “new life,” without it being his idea in the first place. 

I guess what I’m trying to say is that she might have done it if he asked, but he didn’t. He seemed content with dying and didn’t fear it.
I appreciated Dogtooth more than I liked it. The Favourite is my most enjoyed.

>I mean personally I read the film as a socialist work first and foremost.

That was an issue I had with the film. I felt the socialism was underexplored. Those who have read the book tell me it is a much stronger theme in the book.

I’m sure it had a stronger emphasis in the book but I also think that a core aspect of the film is the way personal development and social development are inherently interconnected and Bella’s development as a person is meant to be analogous with social development. But that’s just my reading

You may have lost me. I thought you were saying socialist and personal development as two different points. I agree with you on her personal development. But for socialism, I thought you were talking about her attending socialist meetings and talking about labor rights.
In the film Bella’s development as a person is meant to mirror the way our develops collectively as a society via socialism.

As far as the title goes, I think that it’s about people’s perception of innocence. We look at someone like Bella at the start of the film, and go “aw, poor thing, she doesn’t know any better.” Innocence is perceived as a weakness. However, I think this is a problem with the tainted mind, one without innocence. Her innocence is truly one of her great strengths. It opens her up to the world and to exploration, and propels her growth. Someone else said that men are the true poor things, and they do seem to have the more tainted minds, but I think it’s just a broad statement on innocence and perspective. Bella was never the Poor Thing, anyone who viewed her as such was.

It’s definitely a movie I need to watch again, as I was so taken back by the visuals that I wasn’t fully introspective on the themes. That being said, the positivity comes through this idea of looking for the wonder in everything, and how beautiful the world can be if you choose to see it as so. This is a choice Bella gets confronted with through the nihilist guy, and although it grounds her, somewhat tainting her innocence, she still brings optimism to the world and uses her growing intelligence to explore opportunities that come to her. I know this is coming a bit late into my writing, (it’s kind of just a train of thought), but I think that it’s also about innocence from bias. Even when she learns more about the world she refuses to judge before seeing for herself, as is the case with her prior husband. Compare that to everybody who’s constantly putting expectations on her.

That’s all, thanks for reading.
That makes sense. I just thought the latter was underdeveloped.

I left the film wondering if it was actually a little bit anti-feminist/misogynistic, or at least poking fun at the concept of the dawn of feminism, for some of the same reasons that you mentioned. The film is almost saying that women were helpless, idiotic invalids prior to thier libertarion (or, rather, making fun of this point of view, if you see what I mean). Also, what do they get from thier libertarion? Lots of sex with gross men? A weird boat trip? Then, at the end, they get to be the queen of the freek animal lab?

I enjoyed the movie, but the idea that it's about the empowerment of women seems suspect.

The socialist meetings feel like a throwaway joke more than a serious theme of the movie. Bella doesn’t really apply her apparent socialism anywhere in her life, content to live in her mansion in the end.

I felt so sorry for Godwin, the way he casually talked about his father mutilating him through those horrific experiments. It touches on the familial lineage of trauma. Bella is both a victim of Godwin, his daughter, his experiment and his loved one. I feel like Bella performing the Godwin like experiment on the man who harmed her/her mother, she is showing how we introject the negative characteristics of our parents but have the freedom to change how we what we with those traits

Poor Things explores what happens when a captive person becoming free from captivity. I think a lot of the same themes are explored in his earlier work Dogtooth and Poor Things. Family/lineage, captivity, sex, social conventions, power and control. I think he is right that Poor Things is his most positive film. There is no way this film would be as popular as it is if it wasn’t one of his more positive films. 

This post reminds me that when I saw The Killing Of A Sacred Deer in theater, multiple people walked out.

Glad others are seeing this, too. It's probably the fatal flaw for the movie for me. When the gun is pulled on her we know with absolute certainty that nothing will happen to her based on the absolute lack of consequences established for her character throughout the film. I don't think you can have a successful narrative/story without consequences. It just doesn't work. While the movie definitely had some laughs and was a spectacle, this is where it just didn't work, like at all. 

OP, for what it's worth, this is my least favorite Yorgos movie personally. Maybe try another?

He’s a member of what is dubbed the Greek Weird Wave which often is absurd for absurdity’s sake. Personally, it’s one of my favorite kinds of humor. Poor Things and The Favourite are collaborations with Tony McNamara. I wonder if that’s why they are less overall absurd than many of his other films. The Favourite contains certain absurd points that can seem out of place in comparison. I enjoy the weird vibe it creates.

Yes! Like, call me old-fashioned, but I like stories that have stakes for the same reason I like music that has a melody...it just tends to work. And having stakes doesn't mean it has to be hyper-serious or action-packed. "Little Miss Sunshine" has stakes. "Toy Story" has stakes. Anyway, I digress...

I took issue, at first, with your flippant use of “obviously retarded” to describe the protagonist.

Then I read the rest of your post and I couldn’t argue that “obviously retarded” is sometimes the perfect way to describe something.

I’m not really opposed to Bella’s choice (it’s about self-discovery and autonomy anyway), it’s just disappointing that after all the socialist hints and her avowed aim to change the world, she ends up selfish and embraces her cruelty and yearns to control others just like how others yearn to control her when they have the upper hand.

The lack of real consequences during her journey makes it worse. It seems like rather than acquiring power from personal experiences as Madame Swiney suggests and makes her own way, Bella simply underwent an artificial transformation that leads her to the ironic final state. To me the ending is a relentless mockery of our hope to turn into good people as all human beings are just poor things — we’re either exploited or rotten.

It’s clearly a sped up metaphor for childhood, adolescence and coming of age. As a child, your views about sex and the world are shaped by those in charge of your life, then you break out of that shell and begin to question the things taught to you due to your real world experience. Then at a certain point in life you return to the “village” and determine which aspects of your upbringing to embrace and which ones to abandon. It’s as much about the journey to autonomy for anyone, just viewed through the common (and obviously elevated) trajectory of a woman’s experience. 

I don’t think there’s any reasonable interpretation to support that pre-enlightenment women are invalids. I know you’re only saying it “could” be taken that way, but I think it’s a willfully bad faith reading.

I don't think it's intended as a joke given she makes a brief attempt to apply it to the brothel. People tell me it is a more important part of the book. I think I would have liked it explored more, though maybe the director was right to cut it down.

It’s late today but I’m willing to try The Dogtooth tomorrow. The premise is interesting, the film itself should be good based on Poor Things, and I’d like to see how Lanthimos’ other works are like to decide how to interpret this one lol.

I don't feel like she's always saved by luck/men; it's been a while since I watched it, but from what I remember, the two times she's in any real major real danger - when she's stranded and broke in France, and when her husband confronts her at the end - she gets out of it on her own by working at a brothel to support herself and fighting back against her husband and causing him to accidentally shoot himself, respectively.

Yeah, give it a try. The lack of consequences for the main character in Poor Things is actually way off brand for him. Most of his characters face deep, dreadful consequences, which might be what he means by this being the most hopeful film. Just fyi. Lol.
I mean the word directly comes from Max’s line, which is how she’s seen by others in the early stages. I don’t use it in real life but it’s your freedom if you like.
All successful stories have stakes, because life has stakes.
Oh okay that’s fair. I retract that statement about your post being obviously retarded.

It is definitely about all that stuff too, but I don't think it's an accident that it's set at the dawn of feminism, and is based on Frankenstein, by Mary Shelley, a feminist icon. Feminism is a big part of the story here imo, I'm just not sure what the director is trying to say about it.
Who are these other weird Greek directors? I would love to know

>To me the ending is a relentless mockery of our hope to turn into good people as all human beings are just poor things — we’re either exploited or rotten.

Hah! Now wouldn't this make the final scene extremely ironic? With the hilariously cozy and triumphant tone, with that blaring and booming final fanfare by Jerskin Fendrix? Very interesting reading, thank you for bringing that up.

>she ends up selfish and embraces her cruelty and yearns to control others just like how others yearn to control her when they have the upper hand

I wouldn't personally read it that way. She didn't actually hurt Alfie, quite the contrary - she brought him to the Baxter Mansion after he'd accidentally shot himself, tried to shot her and been a dick to everything within a 5 mile radius. She helped save his life and turned him into a creature that lived peacefully on its own and meant no harm. I'd say that plays into the themes of improvement.

As for socialism, Harry Astley told her not to buy into it. She was impressionable at that time, it's possible she took that to heart.

In France she had been working in the brothel (although not set up to be long term) before she gave Duncan the emergency fund and got officially broke. She continued working there after that. So maybe not facing no consequences at all, but at least I think she being broke failed to hit as a real predicament here, as she didn’t reflect and do things differently accordingly.

And for the ex-husband I take the danger as “being confined in a house with a guy who has weapon and servants and was going hurt her at the night”, and the way she won was “had done nothing effective until the guy approached her and successfully disarmed the guy who was holding a gun with a cup of chloroform while showing an uncooperative attitude all along”, which I take as power of luck. People may have different threshold though. I think it’s acceptable to luck to a happy end but it becomes disturbing if the main character hasn’t done other things by themselves in the past either.
[removed]

It’s a pretty straightforward, life affirming story. I think you should log out of TVTropes and experience cinema. “Plot armor”? What are you even talking about? Do you approach every movie you see as a puzzle you have to outsmart? 

Bella had zero privilege. She repeatedly hit a wall in polite society for about the entire runtime of the film. No one took her seriously, listened to her thoughts, or allowed her to express herself. She goes on a fairly standard journey of self discovery, including rejecting her creator to find out the ultimate truth of where she came from and who she was (what you described as her husband “randomly” showing up), which also turned out to be just another miserable situation for a trapped woman.

I think you’re missing the point of the film if you analyze each situation for a “realistic” out. Bella getting attacked in a heightened, fantasy version of Lisbon would do what? Bella acknowledging the Madame snapping at Toinette instead of her would do what? Did you remember Harry telling Bella she can’t help the poor in Alexandria? Should the movie have stopped to dig into the socioeconomic conditions of the obviously fantastical, allegorical version of Alexandria? That would be an awful movie. 

The film is about life. It’s not supposed to be a perfect checklist of correct attitudes where every character does the “right” thing. If you felt nothing from the film, you might need to revisit it down the road when you’re out of your head and not in your own way.

It just falls flat for me for whatever reason. Which is strange because I normally adore absurd, eccentric and weird. 

Maybe it’s that those choices sometimes make the characters feel distant as a result? I can’t help but see the director manipulating the scene to be absurd rather than allowing the characters to play off each other naturally. 

Or maybe it’s that there’s not a straight man to call attention to how the absurd really is absurd in this world too. And if the whole world is to be absurd, maybe I just don’t find the tone to match in a way that satisfies me. 

I don’t know. Just some random thoughts.
# Athina Rachel Tsangari, Babis Makridis, Christos Nikou, some say Yannis Economides but I think his style differs, Alexandros Avranas.

Yeah, it's just that in both those examples, things work out strangely perfectly for her right away, without a struggle. She doesn't have to face any aggression in the brothel (unless you count the madam's "love bites"); in fact, she's treated kindly and given a big room and plenty of free time. And with the ex-husband, she just throws the drink in his face and boom, done. It just felt like a series of Chekov's guns that never went off...
what is going on with my font?
Right, OP wrote all of that when the real explanation is that he hasn’t seen the rest of the director’s work.

> As for socialism, Harry Astley told her not to buy into it. She was impressionable at that time, it's possible she took that to heart.

After donating Duncan’ money, Bella went for Harry. Harry told her he’s sorry that he showed her the slum with the intention to hurt her. Bella said she believed she could improve the world, Harry said no, and Bella said he’s a broken little boy and left, saying she believed things could go better. Her enthusiasm continued in Paris. I thought she’s clearly an idealist up until the wedding. She didn’t buy what Harry said at all, even though he seems like the one with truth if you agree with my interpretation of the film.

> She didn't actually hurt Alfie, quite the contrary - she brought him to the Baxter Mansion after he'd accidentally shot himself, tried to shot her and been a dick to everything within a 5 mile radius. She helped save his life and turned him into a creature that lived peacefully on its own and meant no harm. I'd say that plays into the themes of improvement.

It’s interesting that you bring up the theme of improvement. Bella kept talking about that since she read with the old madame on the ship. She told Harry she started to get annoyed at Duncan and had cruel thoughts, and despite him claiming that all are cruel, she disagreed and wishes not to be cruel, so she had to improve on that aspect. She talked about how she’d like to improve the world in Paris. She mentioned that she had been a sex worker and asked Max if he believed people were improbable before she proposed to him. And the next and final time she talked about improvement was to give the ex-husband a goat brain. It’s worth noting that this was the only improvement fulfilled in the film, through an act that I’d argue was cruel, which reminded me of early Bella stabbing corpses in God’s laboratory.
I didn't think it was truly cruel - it saved Alfie's life and rid him of his despicable traits.
Okay then, people have different perspectives, but I think this being the only improvement actually done despite the recurring theme is a clear irony anyway
Yes, it is kind of ironic. And maybe indicative of Lanthimos' pessimistic sensibilities.
Thanks, while there are still dissonances that bug me, the take on innocence is interesting and I could see why people appreciate it

I simply don't know what to take of that ending. I mean, yeah they didn't kill him, right? Bella did NOT wanted to kill someone. But oh, they put his brains on a goat's body. What is that, a lifelong punishment?

It simply strikes me as so cruel and inhumane, as if it was written just for the audience's laughs. On the other hand, I'm willing to believe it has to do with abused-victim-inflicts-abuse type of situation, or maybe it's something I don't get from Poor Things's fucked up world.
Your effort to not give credit to her actions is almost commendable. Almost.
God's dad was pretty much a sociopath. God was a victim of his father who nonetheless did his best. Bella was an experiment of God who already at a young age seems wiser than God.

Dogtooth is his one film I haven't seen. I started it, but shut it off when the cat got tossed. I keep thinking I should try it again but I'm still kinda scared. I love The Lobster, KOASD, The Favorite.
I don't know if the film is *about* feminism so much as it is a very creative *portrayal* of it.

The exploited win their freedom through enlightenment and class struggle and reshape the world that they live in built around freedom, logic, equality, and Marxism. 

That’s incredibly hopeful.

I don’t think it does anything to attack someone and accuse them of failing to feel something from a piece of art because of a failure on their part.

It’s not going to make them think differently about the work, but it is going to make them think their thoughts are met with derision and condescension and are less likely to share going forward. 

Besides, if everyone felt the same way towards all art, it would be a pretty boring subject to discuss.

I didn't like this movie, and I've posted about this film in other threads as well. I never got a sense that Bella learned anything from anyone. Instead, her growth came from her own natural tendencies, not from any other person. There is no point at all to the sex scenes, and they never taught her anything or what to avoid...rather, they just "happen".

The story challenges the norm of British conservative culture and manners and shows that these are culturally designed, imperfect, and biased towards a particular hegemonic interest. It shows tried to show that science and study is rejected in favour of religion and tradition. Strongly disagree that it’s just an exercise in cynicism.
Yeah I didn't love the cat scene either. For me there weren't any worse scenes after that, if it helps.
I mean half was riffing while I went so it’s alright to bug ya a bit, I think I’m onto smth though
Yeah I remember the plot, so, your point? That Bella giving another human a goat brain is wholesome? I genuinely don’t get it.
It’s based off a book called poor things

>It’s worth noting that this was the only improvement fulfilled in the film, though dubious and through an act I’d argue was cruel (sure the guy was evil and wasn’t bleed to death but his brain and the goat’s body disappeared and do you really think it’s fine to keep a human body like that for one’s own amusement?), which reminded me of early Bella stabbing corpses in God’s laboratory.

Yeah, striked me as odd and cruel... how is it suppossed to be a way of "keeping Alfie alive", if she literally swapped brains with a goat. At the end scene, you could say that we have the guy's corpse—Alfie isn't there, he's fucking dead. The only thing in there is the goat's consciousness.

I'm not really sure what Lanthimos is trying to dude here... did he tried to do a lame joke? = cutting to a shot of a goat to get a laugh from the audience, and as you said, amusement for the characters.

On other hand, I'm willing to believe that it perhaps has to do with a abuse-victim-inflicts-abuse-on-others type of thing, where we see Bella replicating the things that were done to her, not being able to notice the abuse or something.

Idk, I'm so confused.
It’s such a powerful film. It changed my perspective on so much and I still find myself thinking about it. It does so much, such a punch. 10/10.

I agree. I feel like such a snob saying people are "watching things wrong" but lately there has been an influx of posts with this cinema sins vibe, like you can tell they go into every movie trying to outsmart it. While being stuck in this very conventional (I guess I'd call it) outlook of what "plot" should be.
I outlined pretty clearly the improvement across generations. For some reason you're fixated on the villain being turned into yet another experiment whereas he's a fairly minor plot point.

How many humans learns lessons or what to avoid in the future through sex? What’s the point of sex? Most sex that happens in life is pointless, just a vain attempt at fulfillment and a fruitless desire to get rid of an uncomfortable sensation/urge.

Of course the visual storytelling is incredible and I expected this to become a favorite film, but... When I realized in the first 10 minutes it was about a human with a fully grown woman's body and the brain of a child I turned off. Every straight man's wildest fantasy come true. Getting all you desire physically without a fully formed, thinking brain to get in your way. And then the (nearly) ONLY woman in the movie (parity, please) goes on a quest, not to fulfill her own needs, but to ultimately fulfill the needs of the many men in her life. Seriously, where are the other women? Have we not leaned there could be much more depth to mine if we just made one of these other central characters a woman? Hollywood loves to subjugate women and they will fall all over themselves for a woman producer/ star who participates in her own subjugation.

You mean Godwin’s father > Godwin > Godwin’s daughter (Bella) demonstrates an improvement across generations in the sense that the younger are more capable to love and care? 

Sure but Godwin’s second creation, Felicity, is a clear backslide compared to Bella, and it seems that Bella doesn’t do anything about that (e.g. encourage her to explore the world and get mature) in the end either. So this framing lacks consistency.

Plus the film focuses on Bella’s journey, and the improvements I’m talking about - when the word improvement shows up in the lines - are about future Bella comparing to early Bella, and future world comparing to status quo (brothel’s rules, the poor, Felicity’s condition etc.) 

I talk about the ex-husband because I think the plot is important. Bella was an idealist who wanted to make the world a better place at the wedding. She lived a wealthy life without doing anything helpful (except taking her friend out of the brothel) in the end. It’s contradictory, so clearly something happened in between. This leaves us to the visit to the ex-husband’s house. I take it as Bella rediscovering her cruelty (there’s a conversation on that.)

Just like the word improvement, the word cruelty shows up several time throughout the film. Harry said the improvement through philosophy is people trying to run away from the fact we are cruel beasts. Born that way, die that way. (He showing Bella the slum in the hope to hurt her showcased his own cruelty.) 

This turned out to be disturbingly true. You talk about the Baxters across generations, so let we see: 

Godwin’s father was, as you say, pretty much a sociopath. So, borne cruel and died cruel. 

Godwin was introduced as a crazy scientist, was cruel to Bella (confined her, hit and incapacitated her the first time they went out), gradually turned her loose and became more of a loving and caring figure, but it didn’t take long for him to create another Bella and be even more cruel to this one til his death. 

Bella was cruel in her early stages (killed the frog and stabbed the corpse), but as she grew while she still had cruel thoughts, she said she didn’t want to be like that and must to improve on that aspect. Looks good, if the ending was not she dismissing all the words she had on the desire to improve and doing cruel things nonchalantly.

This is why I don’t know how could the film be hopeful at all.

Just watched The Dogtooth and it’s a great film. It’s definitely unpleasant to watch but the story doesn’t disturb me like the colorful and shiny Poor Things does. I’d say I even feel more hope from The Dogtooth (I doubt the ending is a successful escape but still) than from Poor Things. Maybe my interpretation of Poor Things is really far from the director’s intention, but I’m not sure how to make sense from it otherwise.

Bella is not fulfilling her own needs? What movie did you watch?

Truest comment ever
Various angles... Sex, sex, sex, oh and sex!
Did you miss the scenes of her exploring Lisbon, different food, going to parks and rediscovering her previous life?
